prompt: Why doesn't the Ω(n log n) comparison-sort lower bound apply to Radix Sort?
options: Radix Sort is actually O(n log n) too, so it's irrelevant
Radix Sort never directly compares two elements against each other
Radix Sort only works on already-sorted input
The lower bound only applies to recursive algorithms
explanation: The Ω(n log n) bound is specifically a lower bound for comparison-based sorts. Radix Sort distributes by digit value instead of comparing elements, so it's exempt.

prompt: In LSD Radix Sort, which digit is processed in the very first pass?
explanation: LSD = Least Significant Digit first; the first pass sorts by the 1s place.

prompt: Sorting n b-bit numbers with r-bit digit groups costs O((b/r)*(n+2^r)). If b <= log(n), what is the optimal choice of r?
options: r = b (a single digit covering the whole number)
r doesn't affect the runtime in this regime
explanation: With r=b, the runtime becomes O(n + 2^b), and since b <= log(n), 2^b <= n, giving O(n) -- a single pass over one full-width digit is optimal in this regime.

prompt: Is Radix Sort's correctness guaranteed if an individual digit-pass uses an UNSTABLE sort (e.g. bucket order via a LIFO stack)?
options: No -- an unstable digit-pass can reverse relative order and undo the correctness of previous passes
Yes -- stability doesn't matter since each pass only looks at one digit position
Yes, as long as the final pass (most significant digit) is stable
It depends only on whether the numbers have distinct digit values
explanation: RadixSort relies on each pass PRESERVING the relative order established by earlier (less significant) passes -- an unstable pass can silently break this and produce an incorrectly sorted result.
